clue.text: Despicable note the PM can't be troubled about

indicators.note: troubled suggests stirred up and 'about' suggests turned round, so the letters of the phrase before are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A scornful remark about a Prime Minister who can't be bothered with anything.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubled about' tells you to rearrange all fifteen letters of NOTE THE PM CANT BE; the apostrophe in can't is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: Something so low it does not even deserve scorn is utterly despicable.

clue.text: The Wedding March is not for him!

definitions.text: The Wedding March is not for him!

parts.words: The Wedding March is not for him!
parts.note: read as a bachelor who avoids weddings, but the man meant holds a degree in music, for whom Mendelssohn's march is simply a piece to study

explanation.surface: A confirmed single man shudders at the sound of the bridal music.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a man avoiding marriage; the twist is that 'for him' also points to an academic degree whose holder studies music like the Wedding March.
explanation.definitionFit: A music graduate holds a university degree in the subject, and the unmarried man in the title fits the anti-wedding joke.

clue.text: Month before Fitzgerald produced a story

parts.note: NOV is the usual abbreviation for November
Ella Fitzgerald, the American jazz singer

explanation.surface: In the month before, the writer Fitzgerald turned out a new tale.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pulls you towards F. Scott Fitzgerald the novelist, but the Fitzgerald wanted is the singer Ella.
explanation.definitionFit: A short novel is a kind of prose tale, longer than a short story.

clue.text: Should it always include marines?

indicators.note: include asks for the word for always to hold the marines inside it

parts.note: AY (aye) is an old word meaning ever or always
RM stands for Royal Marines

explanation.surface: A question of military policy: should the land forces always have a marine contingent?
explanation.walkthrough: AY is an old word for 'ever' (as in 'for aye'). The whole clue works as the definition too: a land force that has the Royal Marines inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A land fighting force is the body asked about, and here it literally contains the Royal Marines.

clue.text: Don't dry washing inside lodgings

explanation.surface: Advice not to dry clothes indoors, plus a note about where you stay.
explanation.definitionFit: Hanging laundry outdoors is the alternative to drying it indoors; a place you frequent or live is a haunt or digs.

clue.text: Ex-pupil's remedy is hard to understand

parts.note: an ex-pupil is an Old Boy, OB, and the apostrophe-s gives OBS
a remedy is a cure

explanation.surface: A former student's cure for something proves baffling.
explanation.definitionFit: Something obscure is unclear or difficult to grasp.

clue.text: Duck pate always contains it

indicators.note: contains says the letters sit inside the run of words pate always

explanation.surface: A duck pâté is always made with duck meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'contains' says the answer is inside the words 'pate always', reading paTE ALways.
explanation.definitionFit: This small freshwater dabbling bird is a species of wild duck.

clue.text: The name applied to a gas

indicators.note: applied, in the sense of put to work in a different arrangement, signals the letters of the phrase are rearranged

explanation.surface: A chemist gives a name to a newly discovered gas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'applied' tells you to rearrange the seven letters of THE NAME.
explanation.definitionFit: Marsh gas, the main component of natural fuel gas, is a simple hydrocarbon.

clue.text: Survived the crisis, but went round the bend

explanation.surface: Someone pulled through a crisis but has gone mad in the process.
explanation.definitionFit: Passing a critical point in an illness or crisis; literally steering round a bend in the road, where 'round the bend' suggests madness.

clue.text: Beware males who are primitive

definitions.note: used as a noun, primitive people, matching the plural answer

parts.note: cave is Latin for beware, used as a schoolboy warning
males are men

explanation.surface: A warning to watch out for brutish men.
explanation.walkthrough: CAVE (pronounced kay-vee) is old British public-school slang, from Latin, for 'look out!'.
explanation.definitionFit: Stone Age people living in rock shelters are the stock image of early, undeveloped humans.

clue.text: Small talk makes little splash

parts.note: patter is glib, rapid talk

explanation.surface: Idle chatter makes hardly any impact.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests small talk as one phrase; 'Small' is just S and 'talk' is PATTER.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprinkling of drops or a minor spray is a small splash.

clue.text: Three-quarters netted large fish

indicators.note: netted means caught inside, so the compass letters hold the abbreviation for large

parts.note: the four compass points are quarters; three of them here are E, E and S

explanation.surface: Most of the catch is made up of big fish.
explanation.walkthrough: In crosswords 'quarter' can mean a compass point (N, S, E, W), so three quarters are three such letters: E, E, S, which round L give the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: These snakelike creatures, the eel family, are fish.

clue.text: Symposium shows union leader is in trim

indicators.note: is in says the union's first letter is placed inside the word for trim

parts.note: in trim means in good form, so trim is form

indicators.note: leader picks out the first letter of the word union

explanation.surface: A conference shows the union boss is fit and well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'union leader' looks like a trade-union boss, but it just gives U, which goes into FORM.
explanation.definitionFit: A forum is a meeting place or assembly for public discussion, like a symposium.

clue.text: People's competition

explanation.surface: A contest open to the general public.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', linking the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: An ethnic group or nation is one sense; a speed contest is the other.

clue.text: Lively young lady full of sex appeal

indicators.note: full of says the name holds the other piece inside it

parts.note: Val is a girl's name, standing for a young lady
IT is old slang for sex appeal, from the 1927 film It

explanation.surface: A spirited young woman bursting with allure.
explanation.definitionFit: Vital can mean full of energy and animated.

clue.text: I entered shallow marine inlet

indicators.note: entered says the letter I goes inside the word for a shallow

parts.note: a ford is a shallow crossing in a river

explanation.surface: Someone describes wading into a shallow sea inlet.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiord (fjord) is a long narrow arm of the sea between cliffs.

clue.text: Resolved to dine without a lot of food

definitions.text: Resolved to dine without a lot of food

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means the rearranged letters go round a
resolved, read as solved again, signals the letters of to dine are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A slimmer has made up their mind to eat only small meals.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resolved' rearranges TO DINE into ONDIET, and 'without' (outside) puts that around A. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A slimmer has decided to eat little, which is what restricting food intake means.

clue.text: Urgent information given during departure

indicators.note: given during says the information is placed in the middle of the word for departure

parts.note: an exit is a departure
GEN is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Important news is handed over as someone leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is British slang for facts or information.
explanation.definitionFit: Exigent means pressing or demanding immediate attention.

clue.text: Not even graduate trainees can be bizarre

parts.note: odd numbers are not even
BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate
L is a learner, so two learners give LL

explanation.surface: An uneven number of new graduate recruits can seem strange.
explanation.walkthrough: L stands for a learner (as on British learner-driver plates), so plural trainees give LL.
explanation.definitionFit: An eccentric person or thing is strange or weird.

clue.text: Contract to give players their cards

explanation.surface: A card game where an agreement is made over the hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is striking an agreement; the second takes DEAL literally, giving cards to players.
explanation.definitionFit: Agree a business bargain; distribute playing cards.

clue.text: Purification after five years of desire and spirit

parts.note: lust is strong desire
rum is a spirit, a strong alcoholic drink

explanation.surface: Cleansing oneself after half a decade of lust and drink.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Rome a ceremonial cleansing of the people followed the census held every quinquennium.

clue.text: Rust taken from bar in the centre

indicators.note: in says the word for bar is placed within the word for centre

parts.note: the core is the centre
a rod is a bar

explanation.surface: Rust removed from an iron bar in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: To corrode is to eat away metal, as oxidation does.

clue.text: Each new writer is lower in reputation

indicators.note: new signals that the letters of the word each are put in a fresh order

parts.note: a pen is a writing instrument

explanation.surface: Every newly published author is held in lower esteem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges EACH to CHEA, then PEN is added.
explanation.definitionFit: To degrade or debase is to make something less respected.

clue.text: Old copper with inclination to be a medic

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a list is a lean or tilt, as of a ship

explanation.surface: An elderly policeman with a desire to become a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'copper' suggests a policeman, but it is the metal, symbol Cu.
explanation.definitionFit: An eye doctor is a medical specialist.

clue.text: Hungry chap makes complaint

annotationWithheld.why: Hungry chap makes complaint: MOAN is MAN round O, but the only word for O (empty) is Hungry, which would also have to be the container signal, one word doing two jobs

clue.text: Escort for hard-hearted employer

indicators.note: hearted says the letter for hard goes into the heart of the word for employer

parts.note: a user is one who employs something
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone looking for a companion to accompany a tough boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard-hearted' looks like one adjective meaning callous; split it, and H goes into USER.
explanation.definitionFit: An usher shows people to their seats, leading them as an attendant.

clue.text: A game played by Kennedy

explanation.surface: A board game played by someone named Kennedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Ludovic Kennedy, a British broadcaster and writer, was known as Ludo.
explanation.definitionFit: A children's board game with dice and counters; the nickname of broadcaster Ludovic Kennedy.

clue.text: Adam's first home in Avon

explanation.surface: The first man's original home is in a county in the West of England.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Eden, British Prime Minister, became Earl of Avon; Avon is also an English river and former county, the false trail.
explanation.definitionFit: The garden in Genesis was where the first humans lived; the statesman ennobled as Earl of Avon.

clue.text: Where to find section of the Burma-Siam railway

definitions.text: Where to find section of the Burma-Siam railway

indicators.note: section of tells you that the letters needed are a part cut from inside the words Burma-Siam

explanation.surface: Where the wartime Burma-Siam railway was built.
explanation.walkthrough: 'section of' says the answer is inside 'Burma-Siam' (burmA-SIAm), and the whole clue also defines the continent.
explanation.definitionFit: Burma and Siam (now Myanmar and Thailand) are in this continent, where the railway runs.

clue.text: One who lays out a linesman

explanation.surface: A football official who also spends a lot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'linesman' looks like a football official, but means a writer of lines: the poet Stephen Spender.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who pays out money; the poet Stephen Spender, writer of verse lines.

clue.text: Intense love involves pains so terrible

indicators.note: terrible suggests something wrecked, so the letters of pains so are rearranged

explanation.surface: Deep affection brings with it dreadful suffering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' rearranges PAINS SO.
explanation.definitionFit: Passion is a strong, overpowering emotion such as ardour.

clue.text: What feminists do to be self-employed?

definitions.text: What feminists do to be self-employed?

parts.words: What feminists do to be self-employed?
parts.note: a woman refusing to treat any man as her boss, which also describes working for oneself with no superior

explanation.surface: Feminists refuse to take orders from men, working for themselves.
explanation.walkthrough: Self-employed people have no boss; feminists reject male authority, so both refuse to acknowledge a superior.
explanation.definitionFit: Refusing to acknowledge any person as one's superior is the idea of independence behind self-employment.
